Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

NEW YORK (CNN) -- Federal, state and municipal agencies staged an elaborate drill in the waters off New York City on Tuesday to prepare for the possibility of a nuclear or dirty-bomb attack from the water. A U.S. Coast Guard vessel passes a container ship in New York Harbor as part of Tuesday's terror drill. "We're a big city, and there are vulnerabilities," said Ray Kelly, commissioner of the New York Police Department. Agencies involved in Tuesday's test  emphasized they did not undertake it because of a specific threat against the city. However, Kelly said the city was taking no chances after a proclamation years ago by Osama bin Laden. "We do know that Osama bin Laden several years ago obtained a fatwah to use nuclear weapons, and our goal is to make certain that that fatwah does not come to fruition," he said. In addition to increasing various agencies' preparedness for a seaborne radiological attack, Kelly said Tuesday's well-publicized drill was meant to deter those who would perpetrate such an attack. "It pays to advertise to a certain extent. We want anyone who would do us harm to know that we're out there, that we have the capability to detect," Kelly said. Eight government agencies participated in the drill, ranging from the NYPD to the U.S. Coast Guard. The exercise took place at the entrance of New York Harbor, just south of the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge linking Staten Island to Brooklyn. Per the drill's plan, eight boats were to cross a checkpoint set up by authorities. They were on the lookout for abnormally high concentrations of radioactivity -- a telltale sign of an improvised nuclear device or a radiological dispersal device, more familiarly known as a dirty bomb. Some of the boats were decoys with no radioactive substances aboard, while others had actual radioactive isotopes planted in them. A radioactivity detector in the hull of the authorities' boats was to identify which vessels had radioactive substances in them. The devices are highly sensitive -- so much so that people who have recently had certain medical treatments can set them off. It was up to the authorities participating in the drill to sort the good boats from the bad -- and to intercept the bad. Only minutes into the six-hour exercise, equipment aboard a police boat detected radioactivity within a small white pleasure craft passing through the checkpoint. Two patrol vessels then converged on the pleasure craft, while officials began to question the driver and his two passengers. Soon after, authorities boarded the boat and used a radiation detector, officially known as a radiological isotope identification detector, to produce a "spectrum" of the radiological material. They then transmitted the spectrum to the Department of Homeland Security's Joint Analysis Center (JAC) in Washington to determine precisely what radiological material was aboard the boat. Within moments, the JAC radioed back with a positive identification: Caesium-137, an industrial radioactive isotope that if used in large enough quantities could power a devastating dirty bomb. Sure enough, when a separate boat containing press and police officers sidled up to the apprehended craft soon afterward, the portable radioactivity detectors of officers onboard began to sound excitedly. NYPD Sgt. Art Mogil said that, in part, the agencies chose to practice on leisure craft to illustrate that radiological weapons could be transported in deceptively benign-looking boats. "It doesn't require a large vessel. A device can be just a few pounds and still be a major threat," Mogil said. James Waters, counterterrorism chief for the NYPD, said exercises like Tuesday's were vital because the stakes involved are so high. "Someone bringing in a radiological or nuclear device would be very serious if not catastrophic," he said. On an average day, not all incoming maritime traffic in New York City is subjected to the radioactivity tests performed at Tuesday's drill. An NYPD official declined to specify what percentage of boats normally undergo such screening.

# NYPD Conducts Waterborne Radiation Detection Drill to Counter Nuclear Threats

**NEW YORK** — The New York Police Department carried out a large-scale counterterrorism exercise this week aimed at detecting a potential nuclear device or dirty bomb being smuggled into the city via its surrounding waterways, officials said.

The drill, which involved harbor units, specialized radiation detection teams, and federal partners, simulated a scenario in which a small vessel attempted to transport radioactive material into Manhattan through the busy waters of New York Harbor.

"New York City remains the number one terrorist target in the country, and our waterways represent a vulnerability we can never afford to ignore," said an NYPD Counterterrorism Bureau official during a briefing at the exercise site. "This drill allows us to test our capabilities in real-world conditions and ensure our officers are prepared for the unthinkable."

## How the Detection Worked

During the exercise, officers deployed a network of radiation detection equipment ranging from handheld devices to sophisticated sensors mounted on patrol boats and worn by personnel. The technology is designed to detect gamma rays and neutrons—signatures associated with radioactive materials that could be used in a nuclear weapon or a radiological dispersal device, commonly known as a "dirty bomb."

"Our detection systems can pick up even trace amounts of radiation from a significant distance," explained a sergeant assigned to the department's specialized nuclear detection unit. "When our sensors alert, our teams can move in, identify the source, and determine whether it's a genuine threat or something benign, like a patient who recently underwent a medical procedure involving radioactive isotopes."

Officers demonstrated how mobile detection units on harbor vessels swept the area, closing in on a "suspect" boat once elevated radiation readings were identified. Teams then used more precise instruments to characterize the material and confirm the nature of the threat.

## Layers of Defense

Officials emphasized that the waterborne drill is part of a broader, layered security strategy that includes land, air, and sea components. The department regularly trains alongside the U.S. Coast Guard, the FBI, and other agencies to coordinate responses across jurisdictions.

"No single agency can protect a city this size alone," the Counterterrorism Bureau official noted. "The coordination you saw today—between our harbor units, our detection specialists, and our federal partners—is what keeps eight and a half million people safe every single day."

The NYPD maintains one of the most robust counterterrorism operations of any local police force in the world, a posture shaped in large part by the September 11, 2001 attacks and the ongoing threat environment in the years since.

## Preparedness in a Changing Threat Landscape

Security experts have long warned that a dirty bomb—which uses conventional explosives to scatter radioactive material—could cause mass panic, economic disruption, and long-term contamination, even if the immediate loss of life were limited compared to a true nuclear detonation.

Officials said drills like this one help the department refine its response times, test new equipment, and identify gaps in coverage before a real emergency occurs.

"We hope we never have to use these skills in a real event," the sergeant said. "But if that day ever comes, the people of this city need to know we're ready."

The NYPD said it will continue to conduct similar exercises throughout the year as part of its ongoing commitment to public safety.

---

**NEW YORK** — Federal, state, and local agencies conducted a large-scale counterterrorism exercise in New York Harbor this week, simulating the interception of a vessel suspected of transporting radioactive material into one of the nation's busiest ports.

The coordinated drill, involving hundreds of personnel and dozens of watercraft and aircraft, was designed to test interagency communication, detection capabilities, and rapid-response protocols in the event of a maritime radiological threat.

## Scenario Overview

According to officials familiar with the exercise, the simulation centered on intelligence indicating that a small commercial vessel entering the harbor was carrying an unspecified quantity of radioactive material intended for a potential "dirty bomb" — a conventional explosive designed to disperse radioactive contaminants.

The scenario unfolded over several hours, beginning with the detection of the suspect vessel by port surveillance systems and radiation-detection equipment. Response teams were then tasked with locating, tracking, and safely interdicting the boat before it could reach a populated area.

## Participating Agencies

## The Interdiction

During the drill's central phase, Coast Guard and NYPD Harbor Unit vessels moved to intercept the simulated threat boat. Tactical teams practiced boarding procedures while specialists deployed handheld and vehicle-mounted radiation detectors to identify and characterize the material aboard.

Helicopters equipped with aerial radiation-sensing technology conducted overflights to map potential contamination zones, while a mock hazardous-materials team demonstrated containment and decontamination procedures.

Role-players portrayed the vessel's crew, allowing tactical officers to rehearse suspect detention and evidence-preservation techniques under realistic conditions.

## Testing Communication and Coordination

Officials emphasized that a primary goal was to stress-test the flow of information among agencies operating across different jurisdictions and communication systems — a challenge repeatedly identified in past emergency responses.

"The threat doesn't recognize agency boundaries or state lines," an FBI representative noted. "Our job is to make sure our response doesn't either."

A joint operations center coordinated the response, integrating live updates from maritime, aerial, and land-based units.

## Community Notification

Authorities had announced the exercise in advance to prevent public alarm, cautioning residents and commuters that they might observe an increased presence of law enforcement vessels, aircraft, and emergency personnel throughout the harbor area.

Officials stressed that there was **no actual threat to public safety** and that no genuine radioactive material was used during the simulation.

Following the exercise, participating agencies planned to conduct after-action reviews to evaluate performance, identify gaps, and refine future protocols.

"Every drill teaches us something new," a DHS official said. "The lessons we take from today directly strengthen our ability to protect this city and this region tomorrow."

# Harbor Security Forces Test Radiation Detection in Joint Dirty Bomb Drill

**NEW YORK** — A flotilla of Coast Guard and NYPD vessels converged on the waters off Staten Island Thursday morning in a large-scale exercise designed to test the region's ability to intercept a radiological threat before it could reach Manhattan's densely populated shoreline.

The drill, dubbed Operation Harbor Shield, simulated a scenario in which intelligence indicated that a radioactive dispersal device — commonly known as a "dirty bomb" — was being smuggled into New York Harbor aboard a commercial vessel. More than a dozen boats and roughly 150 personnel participated in the four-hour exercise.

"The reality is that our harbor sees thousands of vessel movements every single day," said Capt. Michael Reardon, commander of Coast Guard Sector New York. "Our job is to find the one that doesn't belong, and to do it without grinding legitimate maritime commerce to a halt. That's an enormous challenge, and the only way to get it right is to practice relentlessly."

During the exercise, a Coast Guard cutter and two NYPD harbor launches intercepted a "target" vessel — a repurposed fishing boat carrying a small sealed radioactive source used for training purposes. Boarding teams equipped with handheld and body-worn detectors approached the craft, sweeping its hull and cargo hold for telltale gamma and neutron signatures.

Officers relied on a layered detection system. Many crew members wore personal radiation detectors, or PRDs — pager-sized devices clipped to their vests that sound an alarm when radiation levels spike above natural background. To pinpoint and characterize a source, specialized teams carried radioisotope identification devices, or RIIDs, which use sodium iodide and, in some newer models, high-purity germanium crystals to read the specific gamma-ray energy spectrum of a material.

"A basic detector tells you something is there. A RIID tells you *what* it is," explained Lt. Sandra Ellison of the NYPD Counterterrorism Bureau, gesturing toward a handheld unit displaying a spectral readout. "There's a big difference between a medical isotope in someone who just had a cardiac scan and weapons-grade material. We can't shut down the harbor every time a detector chirps. The technology lets us distinguish a real threat from a false alarm in seconds."

Naturally occurring radioactive materials — including cat litter, granite, ceramics and bananas — routinely trigger the sensitive equipment, officials noted, making the identification step essential to avoid disrupting legitimate shipping.

The exercise also tested coordination between agencies, a lesson drawn from the fragmented responses that hampered emergency operations two decades ago. Radiation data collected in the field was transmitted in real time to a joint command post, where analysts from the Department of Energy's Nuclear Emergency Support Team stood ready to advise on isotope identification and containment.

"Interagency communication is the piece that fails first when it isn't rehearsed," said Reardon. "When you have Coast Guard, NYPD, the FBI and DOE scientists all looking at the same threat, everyone needs to speak the same language."

Assistant Chief Robert Cassidy of the NYPD said the department has expanded its maritime radiological detection capabilities significantly in recent years, deploying sensors on patrol boats and at key chokepoints leading into the harbor.

"We consider the water a front door to the city," Cassidy said. "Every drill exposes gaps — a communication delay, a sensor that needs recalibration — and that's exactly the point. We'd rather find those problems today than during a real event."

Officials declined to detail specific vulnerabilities uncovered during Thursday's exercise, citing security concerns, but characterized the operation as a success. A comprehensive after-action review is expected within 30 days, with findings shared among participating agencies to refine future training.

# NYPD, Federal Agencies Conduct Maritime Radiation Detection Drills in New York Harbor

**NEW YORK** — In the waters surrounding Manhattan, a fleet of patrol boats equipped with sophisticated radiation detection equipment moves methodically through the harbor, part of an ongoing effort to guard against one of the most feared threats in the post-9/11 era: a radiological or nuclear device smuggled into the nation's largest city by sea.

New York City police officials, working alongside federal partners, regularly conduct exercises designed to detect radiological materials that could be hidden aboard commercial vessels, recreational boats, or shipping containers passing through the busy waterways.

## A Persistent Concern

The threat of maritime-borne radiological attacks has remained a priority for homeland security officials for years. Intelligence gathered over the past two decades, including from the era when Osama bin Laden directed al Qaeda operations, suggested the terrorist network had aspirations to acquire nuclear or radiological materials. Documents recovered after bin Laden's death in 2011 reinforced concerns among counterterrorism analysts that spectacular attacks against American cities remained a goal of extremist groups.

"We can never assume the threat has passed," a police department official involved in the harbor operations explained. "The waterfront represents both an economic lifeline and a potential vulnerability."

## How the Detection Works

The exercises involve officers equipped with personal radiation detectors—devices small enough to clip onto a belt—as well as boats and helicopters outfitted with more sensitive equipment capable of identifying specific isotopes. The goal is to distinguish between naturally occurring radiation, medical isotopes, and materials that could be used to construct a so-called "dirty bomb," a conventional explosive designed to spread radioactive contamination.

During training scenarios, officers practice approaching and screening vessels, coordinating with the U.S. Coast Guard, Customs and Border Protection, and other agencies that share responsibility for securing the port.

## Layered Security

Officials describe the approach as "defense in depth," with multiple rings of detection extending from the outer harbor to the shorelines of Manhattan. The strategy reflects lessons learned in the years following the September 11, 2001 attacks, when New York became the focal point of American homeland security efforts.
